replies:
Yes, it's reasonable to have him screened. The American Academy of Pediatrics recommends that all children be screened for autism at 18 and 24 months, whether or not anyone has raised concerns. Autism can be hard to spot in toddlers who seem to be developing normally, and screening catches some children who would otherwise be missed.

The usual tool is the M-CHAT-R/F, a short questionnaire you can fill out at a checkup. It takes a few minutes, and your pediatrician will go over the results with you. A positive screen doesn't mean he has autism. It means he needs a more detailed evaluation, and many children who screen positive turn out not to be autistic. A negative screen is also reassuring but not a guarantee, so keep watching his development over time.

You might want to bring up autism at his next well-child visit, or ask for the screen if it's not already part of it. Sooner is worth it if you notice any of these:

- Little or no response to his name by about 12 months
- Little babbling or pointing by 12 to 15 months
- Few or no words by 16 months
- No two-word phrases by 24 months
- Loss of skills he previously had, at any age
- Limited eye contact, or not sharing interest by showing or bringing you things
- Unusual, repetitive movements or intense focus on particular objects

If you ever have a concern, you don't need to wait for a scheduled visit. You can ask your pediatrician for a referral for a developmental evaluation. In the US, early intervention services are available for children under 3 at no cost through your state's program, and most other countries have similar services. Early support makes a difference, so it's better to check and find nothing than to wait and miss something.

The evidence is decent on accuracy but thinner on whether universal screening improves long-term outcomes, and expert bodies disagree. I should have said that in my last answer.

**What's well supported:**
- The M-CHAT-R/F is reasonably accurate in studies. It catches most toddlers who are later diagnosed (sensitivity around 85-90%) and correctly clears most who aren't (specificity around 95% or higher).
- Its positive predictive value is modest. Many children who screen positive don't have autism, often around half or more. A structured follow-up interview, built into the M-CHAT-R/F process, cuts down on false positives.
- Early intervention helps many autistic children. Intensive early behavioral programs have shown gains in some studies, though results vary a lot between children.

**What's weaker:**
- No large randomized trial has shown that screening all toddlers, compared with not screening, leads to better long-term outcomes. The benefit depends on the assumption that earlier identification leads to earlier help and better results, and that assumption is plausible but not directly tested at scale.
- Much of the accuracy data comes from research settings and the tool's developers. Performance can be lower in routine practice, and it may miss some children, especially girls and those with milder presentations.
- Screening has possible harms: anxiety for families, false labels, and follow-up evaluations that turn out to be unnecessary.

**Where expert opinion stands:**
- The American Academy of Pediatrics recommends universal screening at 18 and 24 months.
- The US Preventive Services Task Force (2016) concluded there was insufficient evidence to recommend routine screening in primary care for children without developmental concerns. That's an "I" statement, meaning evidence is inadequate to weigh benefits against harms.

Reasonable people, including pediatricians, come down differently on this. Screening is low-cost and low-risk, so many families choose it. Ongoing developmental monitoring at every checkup matters at least as much as any single screen. If you're unsure, ask your pediatrician what they think and why, since they know your son and their local resources.

DO IT. The screen is quick and low-risk, and the American Academy of Pediatrics recommends it at 18 and 24 months, so it's a reasonable thing to do even though he seems to be developing normally.

The US Preventive Services Task Force concluded in 2016 that there was insufficient evidence to recommend for or against routine screening in primary care for children without concerns. Evidence that screening itself leads to better long-term outcomes is limited. The case for screening rests mainly on the AAP's guidance, the low harms of a brief questionnaire, and the fact that early support helps once autism is identified. The recommendation is reasonable, but it's a judgment call supported by moderate evidence, not a settled proof.
